questions.stem: A neonate has delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent skin and mucosal infections, and notably absent pus formation at sites of infection. The condition is caused by a defect in an adhesion molecule required for neutrophils to exit blood vessels. Which of the following molecules is most likely defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-catenin (CTNNB1)

choices.label: B
choices.text: E-cadherin (CDH1)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frizzled (FZD receptor)

choices.label: D
choices.text: LFA-1 integrin (CD18)

choices.label: E
choices.text: P-selectin (CD62P)

explanation.summary: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency results from a defect in the LFA-1 integrin (CD18), impairing neutrophil adhesion and transmigration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic triad—delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent infections, and absent pus—is leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD). It stems from a defect in the LFA-1 integrin (CD18), which mediates firm adhesion of leukocytes to vascular endothelium; without it, neutrophils cannot transmigrate to sites of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-catenin is an intracellular transcription factor in Wnt/cadherin signaling, not a neutrophil adhesion receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E-cadherin mediates epithelial cell-cell adhesion and beta-catenin signaling, not neutrophil transmigration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Frizzled is the Wnt GPCR, unrelated to leukocyte adhesion and transmigration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P-selectin mediates initial leukocyte rolling, but LAD is specifically due to an integrin (CD18) defect impairing firm adhesion.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher observes that as an epithelial tumor becomes more migratory, its cells internalize E-cadherin. Which of the following best describes the downstream signaling consequence that promotes this migratory, mesenchymal phenotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-catenin is further sequestered at the plasma membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-catenin is released and translocates to the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIF-1-alpha is hydroxylated and degraded by the proteasome

choices.label: D
choices.text: IkB is stabilized, blocking NF-kB activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: STAT proteins are dephosphorylated and retained in the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Loss of E-cadherin releases beta-catenin, which enters the nucleus and reprograms gene expression to support the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cadherin receptors normally sequester beta-catenin at the membrane. When a cell becomes migratory and internalizes E-cadherin, beta-catenin is freed, translocates to the nucleus, binds transcription factors, and shifts the gene expression profile toward movement and migration, facilitating the EMT seen in cancer progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Internalizing E-cadherin releases beta-catenin from the membrane rather than sequestering more of it there.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIF-1-alpha degradation is the oxygen-sensing pathway and is unrelated to E-cadherin internalization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IkB stabilization concerns NF-kB inflammatory signaling, not E-cadherin/beta-catenin behavior.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STAT phosphorylation status is part of JAK-STAT signaling and is not the mechanism of cadherin-driven EMT.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher engineers a hematopoietic cell line to express a cytokine receptor in which every cytoplasmic tyrosine residue has been replaced by phenylalanine. After cytokine is added, the receptor dimerizes normally and the associated Janus kinases become phosphorylated and catalytically active, yet STAT-dependent gene transcription does not occur. Which of the following best explains this failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Janus kinases can no longer associate with the mutated receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phosphorylated STAT dimers are excluded from the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: STAT monomers are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome

choices.label: D
choices.text: STATs lack phosphotyrosine scaffolding sites on the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: The receptor cannot dimerize in response to cytokine binding

explanation.summary: Cytokine receptors must be phosphorylated on cytoplasmic tyrosines to provide the scaffolding sites that localize and enrich STATs for JAK-mediated phosphorylation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Upon ligand binding, JAKs phosphorylate tyrosine residues within the receptor's cytoplasmic region, and these phosphotyrosines serve as scaffolding sites that localize, enrich, and activate other components of the signaling network. STATs are cytosolic monomers that become localized to the membrane receptor during JAK activation; without phosphotyrosine docking sites, STATs are never recruited or phosphorylated, so they cannot dimerize and translocate to the nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states that JAKs are associated, phosphorylated, and active, so JAK-receptor association is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: STATs never become phosphorylated in this system; the defect is upstream of nuclear translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick describes proteasomal degradation of IkB and HIF-1-alpha, not of STAT monomers; STATs simply fail to be recruited here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stem states the receptor dimerizes normally in response to cytokine binding.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: In a wound-healing study, dermal fibroblasts are exposed to transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta). Binding causes the receptor subunits to heterodimerize and activates the receptor's kinase activity. Which of the following best describes the kinase specificity of this receptor and the transcription factors it activates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No intrinsic kinase; Janus kinases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serine/threonine kinase; IkB and NF-kB

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serine/threonine kinase; SMAD proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tyrosine kinase; Grb2 and Ras

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine kinase; STAT monomers

explanation.summary: The TGF-beta receptor is a serine/threonine receptor kinase whose phosphorylation leads to activation of SMAD proteins, gene-specific transcription factors that translocate to the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: TGF-beta binding heterodimerizes the receptor subunits, activating the receptor's serine/threonine kinase activity. Receptor phosphorylation results in phosphorylation and activation of SMAD proteins, which are gene-specific transcription factors that translocate to the nucleus to alter gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lacking intrinsic kinase activity and relying on JAKs describes cytokine receptors; the TGF-beta receptor has its own kinase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IkB and NF-kB belong to the TNF-alpha cascade; the TGF-beta receptor acts on SMADs, not IkB.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grb2 and Ras are recruited by receptor tyrosine kinases such as the EGF receptor, not the serine/threonine TGF-beta receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STAT monomers are phosphorylated by Janus kinases downstream of cytokine receptors, not by the TGF-beta receptor.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Epidermal growth factor binds its receptor on an epithelial cell, causing receptor monomers to dimerize and cross-phosphorylate their intracellular domains. Which of the following signaling components is recruited to the autophosphorylated receptor to activate Ras?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dishevelled

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grb2

choices.label: C
choices.text: IkB kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: SMAD

choices.label: E
choices.text: STAT

explanation.summary: Autophosphorylation of receptor tyrosine kinases such as the EGF receptor colocalizes signaling components including Grb2, which activates Ras.
explanation.whyCorrect: Growth factor binding causes dimerization of RTK monomers and activates their inherent kinase function. Receptor autophosphorylation via cross phosphorylation causes colocalization and activation of signaling components; the brick names Grb2, which activates Ras, and PI3K, which is recruited to generate phosphatidylinositol derivatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dishevelled is the signaling component downstream of the Wnt receptor Frizzled.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IkB kinase phosphorylates IkB in the NF-kB pathway and is not an RTK-to-Ras adaptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMAD proteins are activated by the serine/threonine TGF-beta receptor, not by the EGF receptor to activate Ras.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STATs are transcription factors phosphorylated by JAKs (or select RTKs) and do not activate Ras.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher generates a cell line that expresses no Janus kinase proteins. Surprisingly, stimulation with a growth factor still produces phosphorylated, dimerized STAT proteins in the nucleus. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylated STAT independent of JAK

choices.label: B
choices.text: SMAD proteins replaced STAT as the transcription factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: STAT monomers dimerized without requiring phosphorylation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cytokine receptor phosphorylated STAT using its own kinase domain

choices.label: E
choices.text: The IKK complex phosphorylated STAT in the absence of JAK

explanation.summary: Select STATs can be activated by receptor tyrosine kinases independent of JAK activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although JAKs commonly provide the kinase activity linking hematopoietic cytokine receptors to STATs, the brick notes that select STATs can also be activated via RTKs independent of JAK activity. A growth factor acting through an RTK with intrinsic kinase activity can therefore phosphorylate STAT, permitting dimerization and nuclear translocation even without JAK.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem describes phosphorylated STAT proteins in the nucleus, not SMADs, which are TGF-beta receptor substrates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: STAT dimerization and nuclear translocation follow phosphorylation; the stem states the STATs were phosphorylated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytokine receptors generally lack intrinsic catalytic activity and cannot phosphorylate STAT on their own.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The IKK complex phosphorylates IkB in the NF-kB cascade and is not described as a STAT kinase.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old mountaineer spends three weeks alternating between higher and lower camps while ascending a high peak. Laboratory studies at the end of the climb show a substantially increased red blood cell count. Which of the following molecular events in her kidney most directly accounts for the increased erythropoietin gene transcription?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constitutively active G-alpha-s raises cAMP, driving EPO transcription

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIF-1-alpha escapes hydroxylation and dimerizes with HIF-beta at the HRE

choices.label: C
choices.text: IkB is degraded, freeing NF-kB to bind the EPO promoter

choices.label: D
choices.text: JAK2 phosphorylates STAT monomers that then bind the EPO promoter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolyl hydroxylases hydroxylate HIF-1-alpha so VHL can ubiquitinate it

explanation.summary: During hypoxia, HIF-1-alpha is stabilized, dimerizes with HIF-beta, and stimulates genes containing a hypoxia response element, including EPO.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low systemic oxygen stimulates the kidneys to secrete EPO, and during tissue hypoxia EPO production can rise up to 1,000-fold. Because prolyl hydroxylases are oxygen-dependent, hypoxia prevents hydroxylation, allowing HIF-1-alpha to build up, dimerize with the HIF-beta subunit, and stimulate expression of genes containing a hypoxia response element (HRE) in their promoter. Climbers ascend gradually so the kidneys have time to respond by secreting EPO.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constitutive G-alpha-s activation is the defect in McCune-Albright syndrome and is unrelated to oxygen sensing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IkB degradation releases NF-kB to activate immune response genes downstream of TNF-alpha, not the EPO gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JAK2/STAT signaling is the response of bone marrow cells to EPO, not the mechanism that induces EPO transcription in the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydroxylation and VHL-mediated ubiquitination occur under normal oxygen and keep EPO low; they are suppressed, not activated, at altitude.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with Von Hippel-Lindau disease has developed multiple tumors in several organs. Genetic testing confirms a loss-of-function mutation in the VHL gene. Which of the following best explains why loss of VHL function favors tumor formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated HIF-1-alpha hydroxylation lowers EPO and causes anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of IkB sequestration drives NF-kB inflammatory gene expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Released beta-catenin drives migratory gene expression in all cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stabilized HIF-1-alpha drives GLUT1, angiogenic, and dedifferentiation genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unregulated JAK2 drives constitutive STAT-dependent proliferation

explanation.summary: VHL normally promotes degradation of HIF-1-alpha; without it, HIF-driven expression of high-affinity glucose transporters, angiogenic growth factors, and dedifferentiation proteins favors cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: VHL protein associates with hydroxylated HIF-1-alpha to promote its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. The brick states that VHL mutations cause Von Hippel-Lindau disease largely because VHL regulates expression of high-affinity glucose transporters like GLUT1, growth factors that promote angiogenesis, and proteins that promote cellular dedifferentiation; these collective factors favor cancer formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of VHL prevents HIF-1-alpha degradation rather than accelerating hydroxylation, and the consequence is tumor formation, not anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IkB/NF-kB regulation belongs to the TNF-alpha inflammatory cascade and is not controlled by VHL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: beta-catenin release follows cadherin internalization or Wnt signaling and is not the VHL-dependent mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Constitutive JAK2 activity describes polycythemia vera (JAK2 V617F), not VHL disease.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with polycythemia vera reports that his skin itches intensely every time he takes a warm shower. Which of the following best explains this symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cAMP-mediated melanin deposition in the dermis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess erythropoietin acting on cutaneous nerves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histamine release from abundant mast cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced oxygen delivery to dermal capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: TNF-alpha-driven NF-kB activation in keratinocytes

explanation.summary: Aquagenic pruritus in polycythemia vera results from histamine release by abundant mast cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Polycythemia vera involves JAK2 mutations that increase RBC production as well as overproduction of other select cells. The brick attributes the characteristic skin itchiness after a warm shower to histamine release from abundant mast cells; other symptoms include headaches, tinnitus, blurred vision, fatigue, splenomegaly, and plethora.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cAMP-driven melanin production explains cafe-au-lait spots in McCune-Albright syndrome, not pruritus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Polycythemia vera results from constitutive JAK2 signaling that mimics EPO; the pruritus is a mast cell/histamine phenomenon, not direct EPO action on nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PV increases RBC mass and oxygen-carrying cells; the itching is not an ischemic phenomenon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha/NF-kB signaling underlies inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, not PV-associated itching.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies NF-kB heterodimers in TNF-alpha-stimulated macrophages carrying a mutant subunit. The mutant complex is released from IkB, translocates to the nucleus, and can interact with coactivators, but it fails to localize to the promoter regions of target genes. Which of the following is most likely disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The DNA-binding domain of p50

choices.label: B
choices.text: The kinase activity of IKK-beta

choices.label: C
choices.text: The transactivation domain of c-Rel

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transactivation domain of p65

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ubiquitination of IkB

explanation.summary: Within the NF-kB heterodimer, p50 supplies the DNA-binding domain while p65 (Rel A) or c-Rel supplies the transactivation domain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common NF-kB complex is a heterodimer of p50 and p65 (Rel A); in some scenarios p65 is replaced by c-Rel. The p65 and c-Rel components contain transactivation domains required for coactivator interactions, whereas p50 contains the DNA-binding domain that localizes the complex to promoter regions within targeted genes. A complex that reaches the nucleus and binds coactivators but cannot find promoters has lost p50's DNA-binding function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IKK phosphorylates IkB to release NF-kB; the stem states the complex was released and entered the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: c-Rel, like p65, contributes a transactivation domain, not the DNA-binding function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The p65 transactivation domain mediates coactivator interactions, which the stem says remain intact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IkB ubiquitination and degradation liberate NF-kB, a step that clearly occurred since the complex translocated.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old fair-skinned woman develops a tan and notes that the pain of her sunburn is milder than expected after a day at the beach. Which of the following best describes the initial event in her keratinocytes that ultimately stimulates melanin production in neighboring melanocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: beta-endorphin stimulates melanosome transfer

choices.label: B
choices.text: cAMP activates MITF within the keratinocyte

choices.label: C
choices.text: MC1R on the keratinocyte binds alpha-MSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Melanocyte-derived alpha-MSH binds keratinocyte MC1R

choices.label: E
choices.text: UV-induced DNA damage activates p53 to produce POMC

explanation.summary: UV-mediated DNA damage in keratinocytes activates p53, which drives production of POMC, the precursor of alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Upon UV-mediated DNA damage (e.g., thymidine dimers), the p53 transcription factor is activated in keratinocytes to produce the large pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) protein. POMC is cleaved into peptides including alpha-MSH, a GPCR ligand, and beta-endorphin, which relieves the pain of sunburn. Keratinocyte-derived alpha-MSH then activates MC1R on melanocytes to trigger the cAMP cascade, MITF activity, and melanin synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: beta-endorphin is the POMC-derived peptide that relieves sunburn pain; it is not the trigger for pigment production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: cAMP-driven MITF activation occurs in the melanocyte, downstream of MC1R, not in the keratinocyte as the initial event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MC1R is on melanocytes and is activated by keratinocyte-derived alpha-MSH; the keratinocyte is the source of the ligand, not the receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The direction is reversed: alpha-MSH is keratinocyte-derived and acts on MC1R of melanocytes.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher detects a soluble trimeric form of TNFR-1 in the serum of a patient with active inflammation. Which of the following best describes the origin of this molecule and its effect on TNF-alpha signaling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Overproduced by gene amplification; increases surface TNFR-1 receptor density

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proteolytically cleaved near the membrane; binds TNF-alpha but cannot signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Released by IKK phosphorylation of the receptor; directly degrades cytosolic IkB

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secreted by plasma cells as an antibody; binds and neutralizes TNF-alpha

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shed after receptor ubiquitination; activates NF-kB in neighboring cells

explanation.summary: Proteolytic cleavage of TNFR-1 at a juxtamembrane site releases a soluble trimeric receptor that binds TNF-alpha but cannot transduce a signal, terminating the NF-kB cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: One way the NF-kB signaling cascade is terminated is through proteolytic cleavage of TNFR-1 at a juxtamembrane site. This releases a soluble trimer receptor that is still capable of TNF-alpha cytokine binding but unable to prompt intracellular signals, thereby dampening rather than propagating the response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gene amplification is an overexpression mechanism (e.g., HER2) and would increase membrane-bound receptor, not release a soluble form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IKK phosphorylates IkB; it does not generate soluble TNFR-1, and the soluble receptor does not act on IkB.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha describes adalimumab, a therapeutic, not the endogenous shed receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The soluble receptor arises from proteolytic cleavage, not ubiquitination, and it cannot activate NF-kB because it is no longer membrane bound.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with psoriatic arthritis is started on adalimumab. Which of the following best describes how this drug reduces inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody that binds soluble, circulating TNF-alpha

choices.label: B
choices.text: A small-molecule inhibitor of the IKK ATP-binding pocket

choices.label: C
choices.text: A soluble decoy receptor resembling cleaved TNFR-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: An antagonist that blocks toll-like receptor engagement

choices.label: E
choices.text: An inhibitor of proteasomal degradation of IkB

explanation.summary: Adalimumab (Humira) is a monoclonal antibody (-mab) that binds circulating TNF-alpha with high affinity so the cytokine cannot engage its receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adalimumab is a monoclonal antibody that recognizes soluble, circulating TNF-alpha. The antibody binds TNF-alpha with high affinity, preventing cell signaling because the cytokine is no longer available to bind the cell surface receptor. It is used in inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Small-molecule kinase inhibitors carry the '-nib' suffix (e.g., imatinib); adalimumab is an antibody acting extracellularly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A recombinant soluble decoy receptor resembling shed TNFR-1 describes etanercept (Enbrel), not adalimumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toll-like receptors bind PAMPs; adalimumab targets the cytokine TNF-alpha, not TLRs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adalimumab acts on extracellular TNF-alpha and does not interfere with IkB degradation inside the cell.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher plates fibroblasts on a dish coated with extracellular matrix proteins and observes that the cells attach and spread. Which of the following families of cell surface adhesion receptors is primarily responsible for this attachment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: beta-catenins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cadherins

choices.label: C
choices.text: E-selectins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrins

choices.label: E
choices.text: L-selectins

explanation.summary: Integrins are the adhesion receptor family that binds primarily to the extracellular matrix.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cell surface adhesion receptors are transmembrane glycoproteins that bind either molecules on adjacent cells or components of the extracellular matrix. Of the three principal families, integrins bind primarily to the extracellular matrix, whereas cadherins transbind to cadherins on neighboring cells and selectins function in immune cell trafficking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: beta-catenin is an intracellular transcription factor sequestered by cadherins, not a surface adhesion receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cadherins participate in transbinding, cadherin-to-cadherin across neighboring cells, rather than binding matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E-selectin (endothelial) helps leukocytes adhere to endothelium and is not an extracellular matrix receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: L-selectin (leukocyte) mediates leukocyte hooking onto endothelium during inflammation, not matrix attachment.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies how leukocytes travelling in blood vessels 'hook onto' endothelial cells near an area of inflammation and extravasate. She identifies a selectin that is expressed by both platelets and endothelial cells. Which of the following is this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: E-cadherin

choices.label: B
choices.text: E-selectin

choices.label: C
choices.text: L-selectin

choices.label: D
choices.text: LFA-1 integrin

choices.label: E
choices.text: P-selectin

explanation.summary: P-selectin is named for platelets but is also expressed by endothelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The major selectin types are L-selectin (L for leukocyte), E-selectin (endothelial), and P-selectin (platelet). The brick specifies that P-selectin is also expressed by endothelial cells. Selectins are expressed by cells near areas of inflammation and allow leukocytes and other cells in the bloodstream to hook onto endothelium and extravasate into the inflamed area.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E-cadherin mediates epithelial cell-cell transbinding and beta-catenin sequestration, not leukocyte-endothelial hooking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E-selectin is the endothelial selectin; the brick does not describe it on platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-selectin is the leukocyte selectin, not one expressed by platelets and endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LFA-1 integrin (CD18) is an integrin on leukocytes involved in adhesion to endothelium; it is not a selectin.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Sequencing of a tumor reveals a single amino acid substitution in a receptor tyrosine kinase at a cytoplasmic tyrosine residue that is normally phosphorylated only after ligand binding. The mutant receptor signals continuously in the absence of ligand. Which of the following substitutions most likely explains this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tyrosine to alanine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tyrosine to glutamate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tyrosine to lysine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tyrosine to phenylalanine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine to serine

explanation.summary: A phosphomimetic substitution replaces a phosphorylation-site tyrosine with glutamate or aspartate, mimicking the phosphorylated state and causing continuous receptor activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a phosphorylation site such as a tyrosine within an RTK is replaced by glutamate or aspartic acid, the negatively charged side chain mimics the phosphorylated state. The receptor no longer requires phosphorylation to be active, leading to continuous, ligand-independent activation, an activating (gain-of-function) mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine is a small, uncharged residue and does not mimic a phosphate group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysine is positively charged, the opposite of the negative charge that mimics phosphorylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylalanine cannot be phosphorylated and carries no negative charge, so it cannot mimic the phosphorylated state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine lacks the acidic side chain needed to mimic phosphotyrosine; the brick names glutamate and aspartate as the phosphomimetic residues.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A tumor expresses a receptor tyrosine kinase carrying a single amino acid substitution located far from any phosphorylation site. Biochemical analysis shows the receptor is not phosphorylated, yet it signals constitutively without ligand. Which of the following best explains the receptor's activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accommodating the new side chain stabilizes the active conformation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutation abolishes the receptor's ligand-binding domain

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutation increases the number of receptor gene copies

choices.label: D
choices.text: The substituted residue itself mimics a phosphorylated tyrosine

choices.label: E
choices.text: The substitution enhances transcription from the gene promoter

explanation.summary: Substitutions away from the phosphorylation site can produce conformational changes that mimic the structural change normally requiring post-translational modification, stabilizing the active receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond phosphomimetic substitutions, less intuitive amino acid substitutions can generate constitutively active receptors. A substitution at a site other than the targeted phosphorylation site may cause conformational changes that mimic the structural change typically requiring post-translational modification; despite not being phosphorylated, accommodating the substituted side chain stabilizes the active form of the receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of ligand binding would reduce signaling, whereas this receptor signals constitutively without ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single amino acid substitution changes protein structure, not gene copy number; amplification is an overexpression mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A phosphomimetic residue must sit at the phosphorylation site; the stem places the substitution far from any such site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An amino acid substitution in the protein does not alter promoter activity; promoter mutations are a separate overexpression mechanism.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A tumor shows markedly elevated protein levels of a pro-growth receptor. Gene copy number, promoter sequence, and mRNA levels are all normal, but pulse-chase experiments show that the receptor protein persists in the cell far longer than in normal tissue. Which of the following overexpression mechanisms is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered epigenetic imprinting

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption of protein turnover

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene amplification/duplication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphomimetic substitution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promoter mutation enhancing transcription

explanation.summary: Overexpression of a pro-growth receptor can arise from disrupted protein turnover, which raises receptor levels without any change in gene copy number or transcription.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overexpression of pro-growth receptors excessively amplifies the associated signaling pathway, leading to uncontrolled cell growth. The brick lists four mechanisms: disruption of protein turnover, promoter mutation that enhances transcription, gene amplification/duplication, and alteration in epigenetic imprinting. Normal gene copy number, promoter, and mRNA with a prolonged protein half-life point to disrupted protein turnover.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epigenetic changes such as methylation or histone acetylation alter transcription and would change mRNA levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene amplification would increase gene copy number, which the stem says is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A phosphomimetic substitution is an activating mutation that changes receptor activity, not receptor abundance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A promoter mutation enhancing transcription would raise mRNA levels, which are normal here.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia has cytogenetic testing that demonstrates the Philadelphia chromosome. Which of the following best describes the genetic event that produced it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ABL from chromosome 22 moves next to BCR on chromosome 9

choices.label: B
choices.text: ABL from chromosome 9 moves next to BCR on chromosome 22

choices.label: C
choices.text: BCR from chromosome 9 moves next to ABL on chromosome 22

choices.label: D
choices.text: GNAS from chromosome 22 fuses with ABL on chromosome 9

choices.label: E
choices.text: JAK2 from chromosome 9 fuses with BCR on chromosome 22

explanation.summary: The Philadelphia chromosome forms when ABL on the long arm of chromosome 9 moves next to the BCR gene on the long arm of chromosome 22, the t(9;22) translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gene encoding ABL, a pro-growth non-receptor cytosolic tyrosine kinase, moves from the long arm of chromosome 9 into a new position next to the breakpoint cluster region (BCR) gene on the long arm of chromosome 22. This fusion is called the t(9;22) translocation and creates the hybrid BCR-ABL gene found in all CML cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABL is on chromosome 9, not 22, and BCR is on chromosome 22, not 9.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The chromosomes are reversed: BCR resides on chromosome 22 and ABL on chromosome 9.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GNAS encodes G-alpha-s and is mutated in McCune-Albright syndrome; it is not involved in the t(9;22).
whyWrongByChoice.E: JAK2 mutations (V617F) underlie polycythemia vera; JAK2 is not part of the Philadelphia chromosome.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and cytogenetic analysis of her blasts reveals the Philadelphia chromosome. Her parents, having read that this chromosome causes chronic myeloid leukemia, ask whether the diagnosis is wrong. Which of the following best describes the diagnostic significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It establishes a diagnosis of CML in any leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: It indicates amplification of a receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It indicates an inherited germline predisposition

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is characteristic of CML but also occurs in ALL and AML

choices.label: E
choices.text: It rules out ALL because it is specific to CML

explanation.summary: The Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML but is also seen less commonly in ALL and AML, so its presence alone is not diagnostic of CML.
explanation.whyCorrect: All CML cases exhibit the BCR-ABL fusion gene, but the Philadelphia chromosome is also less commonly seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Therefore the presence of the chromosome is not in itself diagnostic of CML, and a Philadelphia-positive ALL diagnosis is entirely consistent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The chromosome is not diagnostic of CML by itself; the leukemia type is determined by other features.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCR-ABL is a fusion of a non-receptor cytosolic tyrosine kinase created by translocation, not an amplified RTK.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The t(9;22) is an acquired translocation in immune cell progenitors, not an inherited germline mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Philadelphia chromosome does occur in ALL, so it cannot exclude that diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia has been in remission for two years on imatinib and is told her life expectancy now matches that of someone who never had the disease. Which of the following best describes how imatinib halts the growth signal in her leukemic cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody against a BCR-ABL surface epitope

choices.label: B
choices.text: Promotes proteasomal degradation of BCR-ABL protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverses the t(9;22) translocation in progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small molecule occupying the kinase's ATP-binding pocket

choices.label: E
choices.text: Soluble decoy that sequesters the BCR-ABL ligand

explanation.summary: Imatinib (Gleevec), a '-nib' small-molecule inhibitor, blocks the intracellular activation pocket of BCR-ABL so ATP cannot bind, stopping kinase-driven growth signals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imatinib is in the class of small molecule inhibitors indicated by the '-nib' suffix. It blocks the intracellular activation pocket of the kinase, preventing ATP from binding and thus stopping the growth signals typically prompted by kinase activity. Patients in remission after two years of imatinib have the same life expectancy as individuals who never had CML, and the drug also inhibits other pro-growth kinases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Monoclonal antibodies (-mab) such as adalimumab act extracellularly; BCR-ABL is a cytosolic kinase without a surface epitope.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Imatinib inhibits kinase activity by blocking ATP binding; it does not target the protein for proteasomal degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib does not alter the chromosomal translocation; it inhibits the fusion protein the translocation produces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BCR-ABL is constitutively active and has no ligand; a decoy receptor describes etanercept's mechanism against TNF-alpha.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought in for breast development and an episode of vaginal bleeding. Examination shows several hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders on her trunk, and radiographs reveal fibrous dysplasia of the femur. Excess of which of the following hormones most likely accounts for her pubertal findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid hormone

explanation.summary: In McCune-Albright syndrome, precocious puberty in girls, breast development and vaginal bleeding, results from excessive estrogen, the most prominent endocrinopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of precocious puberty, cafe-au-lait spots, and fibrous dysplasia is McCune-Albright syndrome, in which constitutive G-alpha-s activation drives cAMP overproduction and excessive hormone synthesis. Hyperfunctioning endocrine glands cause precocious puberty especially in girls, with breast development and vaginal bleeding at an early age due to excessive estrogen. The brick notes that estrogen is the most prominent hormone involved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisol excess is mentioned as a possible additional endocrine issue but does not explain breast development and vaginal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin drives RBC production and has no role in pubertal development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth hormone imbalances may make affected children taller early but do not drive the pubertal changes described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid hormone abnormalities can occur in McCune-Albright syndrome but are not the cause of precocious puberty.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: The parents of a child recently diagnosed with McCune-Albright syndrome ask two questions: whether their future children are at risk, and why the child's skin lesions and bone lesions are patchy rather than affecting the whole body. Which of the following best answers both questions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosomal translocation acquired in hematopoietic progenitors limits it to blood-derived cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A loss-of-function mutation transmitted from one parent produces variable involvement in offspring

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene amplification restricted to endocrine tissue explains the localized findings and low recurrence

choices.label: D
choices.text: The GNAS mutation is germline and inherited, so every cell carries it and siblings are at risk

choices.label: E
choices.text: The GNAS mutation is somatic and spontaneous, so it is not inherited and not all cells carry it

explanation.summary: McCune-Albright syndrome arises from a spontaneous somatic GNAS mutation, so it is not inherited and, because the mutation is not germline, not all cells are equally affected.
explanation.whyCorrect: McCune-Albright syndrome is not an inherited condition; it arises from spontaneous somatic mutations in GNAS that constitutively activate G-alpha-s. Because the mutation is somatic and not germline, not all cells are equally impacted, which is why manifestations such as cafe-au-lait spots and fibrous dysplasia appear in a patchy distribution.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A translocation in hematopoietic progenitors describes the Philadelphia chromosome and leukemia, not GNAS-driven McCune-Albright syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The GNAS mutation is an activating (gain-of-function) somatic mutation, not a loss-of-function mutation transmitted from a parent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by an activating point mutation in GNAS, not gene amplification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick explicitly states the condition is not inherited and the mutation is somatic, not germline.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with McCune-Albright syndrome is currently taller than his classmates. He sustains a femoral fracture after minor trauma, and imaging shows a lesion in which marrow has been replaced by fibrous tissue. His parents ask what to expect regarding his height as an adult. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He will be shorter because FGFR-3 suppresses endochondral ossification

choices.label: B
choices.text: He will likely be relatively shorter in adulthood because of bone malformation

choices.label: C
choices.text: He will remain taller than average because growth hormone excess persists

choices.label: D
choices.text: His height will be unaffected because fibrous dysplasia spares the long bones

choices.label: E
choices.text: His height will normalize once the fibrous lesions calcify at puberty

explanation.summary: In fibrous dysplasia, children may be taller early due to growth hormone imbalance but end up relatively shorter in adulthood because of bone malformation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome reflects altered stem cell differentiation in which marrow is replaced by fibrous tissue, producing weak bone prone to expansion, thinning of long bones, and fractures. Compared with nonaffected individuals, affected children may be taller early because of growth hormone imbalances during development, but due to bone malformation they will be relatively shorter in adulthood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FGFR-3-mediated suppression of endochondral ossification is the mechanism of achondroplasia, not McCune-Albright syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Early tall stature does not persist; bone malformation leaves affected individuals relatively shorter as adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrous dysplasia adversely impacts the long bones, causing thinning and fractures, as illustrated by this femoral fracture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes no normalization; the weak, expanded bone results in reduced adult height.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Melanocytes are isolated from a cafe-au-lait macule of a patient with McCune-Albright syndrome and cultured alone, without keratinocytes, UV exposure, or added alpha-MSH. The cells nevertheless continue to produce excessive melanin. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constitutive G-alpha-s/cAMP signaling drives PKA and MITF without alpha-MSH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ligand-independent FGFR-3 kinase activity drives MITF expression in melanocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Melanocyte p53 is activated and produces POMC autonomously without UV exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residual keratinocyte beta-endorphin in the medium stimulates pigment production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilized HIF-1-alpha induces melanin genes via the hypoxia response element (HRE)

explanation.summary: In McCune-Albright syndrome, mutant G-alpha-s keeps cAMP elevated, so PKA stimulates melanin production in melanocytes without the need for alpha-MSH acting on MC1R.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally keratinocyte-derived alpha-MSH activates MC1R, a GPCR on melanocytes, to trigger the cAMP cascade, MITF activity, and melanin synthesis. The dermal presentation of McCune-Albright syndrome occurs because constitutively active G-alpha-s overstimulates adenylate cyclase, and the resulting cAMP, via PKA, stimulates melanin production within melanocytes independent of upstream receptor engagement. Cafe-au-lait spots are usually the first manifestation, apparent at or shortly after birth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FGFR-3 activating mutations cause achondroplasia by suppressing chondrocyte proliferation; they are not the McCune-Albright defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p53 activation and POMC production occur in UV-damaged keratinocytes, not autonomously in melanocytes, and there is no UV exposure here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: beta-endorphin relieves the pain of sunburn; it is not the pigment-inducing peptide, and keratinocytes are absent from the culture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIF-1-alpha/HRE signaling responds to hypoxia and controls genes such as EPO, not melanin synthesis.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Two endurance athletes adapt to improve oxygen delivery. One trains at high altitude for several weeks, which raises endogenous erythropoietin. The other performs intense exercise over a single day, which raises 2,3-BPG within red blood cells. Compared with the EPO-mediated response, which of the following best characterizes the 2,3-BPG response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster onset; increases the number of RBCs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster onset; no change in the number of RBCs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Same onset; increases the number of RBCs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slower onset; increases the number of RBCs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slower onset; no change in the number of RBCs

explanation.summary: 2,3-BPG is a glycolytic byproduct made and used within hours to days that enhances oxygen delivery without changing RBC number, whereas EPO acts at the genetic level over days to weeks by increasing RBC production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick contrasts the two adaptations: 2,3-BPG is a metabolic byproduct of glycolysis that is readily made and used (hours to days) but does not alter the number of RBCs. EPO's effect is at the genetic level via hormonal cell signaling, which takes much longer to achieve (days to weeks) and works by enhancing RBC output from bone marrow, increasing total RBC count and oxygen-delivering capacity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG is faster in onset, but it does not increase RBC number; that is EPO's effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The two responses differ markedly in timing, and only EPO increases RBC number.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 2,3-BPG acts faster than EPO, not slower, and it does not change RBC number.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although 2,3-BPG does not change RBC number, its onset is faster (hours to days), not slower, than EPO's.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has plasma glucose measured after an overnight fast. Given that the normal fasting range is 70-100 mg/dL, which of the following measured values is most indicative of hypoglycemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 50 mg/dL

choices.label: B
choices.text: 72 mg/dL

choices.label: C
choices.text: 90 mg/dL

choices.label: D
choices.text: 110 mg/dL

choices.label: E
choices.text: 140 mg/dL

explanation.summary: Fasting plasma glucose below the normal 70-100 mg/dL range indicates hypoglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: After an overnight (basal, post-absorptive) fast the normal plasma glucose range is 70-100 mg/dL. A value of 50 mg/dL falls below this range and represents hypoglycemia, a state that first manifests with CNS symptoms because the brain depends on circulating glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 72 mg/dL sits within the normal fasting range of 70-100 mg/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 90 mg/dL is a normal fasting glucose value.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 110 mg/dL is elevated for a fast (pre-diabetic range 101-125), not low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 140 mg/dL is hyperglycemic for a fasting individual, not hypoglycemic.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A physiologist notes that skeletal muscle stores large amounts of glycogen, yet mobilizing this glycogen during a fast does not raise blood glucose. Which of the following best explains why muscle glycogen cannot contribute to circulating glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skeletal muscle cannot synthesize glycogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Skeletal muscle converts all glycogen directly to lactate before it can be released

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skeletal muscle expresses only GLUT2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skeletal muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skeletal muscle lacks glycogen phosphorylase

explanation.summary: Only the liver expresses glucose 6-phosphatase, so only hepatic glycogen can supply free blood glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucose 6-phosphatase converts glucose 6-phosphate to free glucose, and GLUTs cannot transport phosphorylated glucose. The liver expresses this enzyme so its glycogen-derived glucose exits via GLUT2, whereas skeletal muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and therefore consumes its glycogen locally for catabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscle synthesizes glycogen normally via glycogen synthase; storage is not the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Muscle glycogen is mobilized for local catabolism, not obligatorily converted entirely to lactate for release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT2 is the hepatic transporter; muscle uses GLUT4, but the export block is due to missing glucose 6-phosphatase, not the transporter type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle contains active glycogen phosphorylase and does break down its own glycogen.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought in after beginning to sleep through the night. During these longer fasts the infant develops severe hypoglycemia with pronounced lactic acidosis, and examination reveals hepatomegaly. Symptoms improve with frequent feedings. A deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucokinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphatase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycerol kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hormone-sensitive lipase

explanation.summary: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is a glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Von Gierke disease, glycogen is formed and degraded normally, but liberated glucose is trapped as glucose 6-phosphate because glucose 6-phosphatase is deficient, causing hepatomegaly. Because the liver cannot release glucose, fasting triggers severe hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, and treatment is frequent meals to prevent the fasting state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose entering the liver and would not cause glycogen accumulation with hepatomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycerol kinase is a hepatic enzyme for glycerol handling and does not produce this glycogen-storage picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency impairs glycogen breakdown, but the brick specifically attributes this trapped-glucose, hepatomegaly, lactic-acidosis picture to glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hormone-sensitive lipase acts on adipocyte triglycerides, unrelated to hepatic glycogen and lactic acidosis.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: During a fast, glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogen breakdown but has essentially no effect on skeletal muscle glycogen. Which of the following best explains this tissue selectivity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skeletal muscle cannot generate cAMP in response to glucagon or any other hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Skeletal muscle contains no glycogen to mobilize

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skeletal muscle lacks adenylate cyclase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skeletal muscle lacks protein kinase A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skeletal muscle lacks the glucagon receptor

explanation.summary: Skeletal muscle does not express the glucagon GPCR, so glucagon cannot act on muscle glycogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucagon signals through a GPCR that is present on hepatocytes but absent on skeletal muscle. Because muscle lacks the glucagon receptor, fasting-associated glucagon does not alter muscle glycogen stores; muscle glycogen is instead mobilized by epinephrine, AMP, and calcium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscle readily generates cAMP downstream of epinephrine; the block is the missing glucagon receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Skeletal muscle holds the bulk of the body's glycogen; it simply is not responsive to glucagon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Muscle possesses adenylate cyclase, which is engaged by epinephrine acting through adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscle expresses PKA and uses it in epinephrine signaling.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes liberates glycerol and fatty acids. The glycerol is released into the blood for hepatic use rather than being reincorporated locally. Adipocytes release glycerol because they lack which of the following enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphatase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycerol kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hormone-sensitive lipase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lipoprotein lipase

explanation.summary: Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol from lipolysis cannot be phosphorylated and instead exits the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycerol kinase reversibly forms glycerol 3-phosphate from glycerol and is expressed in the liver, not adipocytes. Because adipocytes lack glycerol kinase, the glycerol released by lipolysis cannot be recaptured and is exported to the liver, which uses it as a gluconeogenic substrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose 6-phosphatase is a hepatic enzyme of glucose metabolism, unrelated to adipocyte glycerol handling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adipocytes do have glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which lets them make glycerol 3-phosphate from DHAP when glucose is abundant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hormone-sensitive lipase is present and is precisely the enzyme carrying out the lipolysis described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipoprotein lipase acts on circulating VLDL/chylomicron triglycerides outside the cell and is not the reason glycerol is released.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old eats a carbohydrate-rich meal, and glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue rapidly increases. This increase results from insulin-stimulated deposition of which of the following glucose transporters at the cell surface?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GLUT1

choices.label: B
choices.text: SGLT1

choices.label: C
choices.text: GLUT2

choices.label: D
choices.text: GLUT4

choices.label: E
choices.text: GLUT5

explanation.summary: Insulin promotes translocation of high-affinity GLUT4 to the surface of muscle and adipose cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin promotes deposition of pre-formed GLUT4 transporters onto the surface of adipose and skeletal muscle. GLUT4 has a low Km (high affinity) for glucose, so its appearance causes rapid glucose uptake that fuels oxidation, glycogen synthesis, and lipogenesis in the fed state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GLUT1 provides basal, insulin-independent glucose uptake and is not the transporter mobilized by insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT1 is a sodium-coupled intestinal/renal glucose transporter, unrelated to insulin-stimulated uptake in muscle and fat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT2 is the hepatic (and pancreatic) transporter that exports glucose and is not insulin-recruited to muscle and fat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT5 primarily transports fructose and is not responsive to insulin in this manner.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A teenager eats a burger, fries, and a milkshake, then sleeps for 13 hours. Compared with the immediate post-meal state, which of the following changes is most expected upon awakening?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased circulating chylomicrons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased hepatic glycogen synthase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased hepatic PFK-2 kinase activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased hormone-sensitive lipase activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased insulin-to-glucagon ratio

explanation.summary: An overnight fast lowers insulin and raises glucagon, activating adipocyte hormone-sensitive lipase.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the overnight fast, insulin falls and glucagon rises (a low insulin:glucagon ratio). Glucagon activates PKA via cAMP, phosphorylating and activating hormone-sensitive lipase to liberate fatty acids and glycerol from adipocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chylomicrons depend on recently ingested dietary fat and decrease after an overnight fast.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucagon-driven PKA phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase, decreasing its activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucagon favors the phosphatase activity of PFK-2, dampening its kinase activity and slowing hepatic glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The insulin-to-glucagon ratio falls, not rises, during a fast.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A man eats a candy bar and, moments later, is startled by an assailant and must flee. Despite the recent high-carbohydrate intake, his blood glucose remains elevated to fuel skeletal muscle. Which hormone is most responsible for overriding insulin signaling in this scenario?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucagon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin

explanation.summary: Epinephrine mobilizes fuel during acute stress independent of blood glucose or insulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epinephrine's metabolic effects mirror glucagon's but occur independent of blood glucose levels. During fight-or-flight, epinephrine overrides insulin signaling to keep glucose elevated, producing cAMP to drive glycogenolysis and hormone-sensitive lipase activity so fuel is available for muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisol supports prolonged stress through gene expression over hours, not the immediate override described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucagon is released when glucose is low; after a candy bar, glucose is high and glucagon secretion would not be driving this response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth hormone is not the acute mediator emphasized here; epinephrine drives the immediate fight-or-flight response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin promotes fuel storage and would lower glucose, the opposite of what is observed.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: During a sprint, a nerve impulse triggers glycogen breakdown in skeletal muscle even without a rise in circulating hormones. Which of the following mechanisms most directly links the nerve impulse to activation of glycogen phosphorylase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium binds calmodulin, which activates phosphorylase kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol induces transcription of glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucagon activates adenylate cyclase in the myocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin stimulates translocation of GLUT4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protein phosphatase dephosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase

explanation.summary: Nerve impulses release Ca2+, and Ca2+-calmodulin activates phosphorylase kinase to turn on glycogen phosphorylase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscle nerve conduction prompts Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This second messenger activates calmodulin, which binds phosphorylase kinase and promotes its activity toward glycogen phosphorylase, driving glycogenolysis for contracting muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol acts over hours via gene expression and does not provide the immediate contraction-linked activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skeletal muscle lacks the glucagon receptor, so glucagon does not act on the myocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin/GLUT4 signaling promotes glucose uptake and storage, not glycogen breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dephosphorylation inactivates glycogen phosphorylase, opposing the mobilization that occurs during a sprint.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A patient has not eaten for several days and is in the prolonged fasting (starvation) state. Which of the following fuels does the brain rely on most heavily under these conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Branched-chain amino acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free fatty acids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycerol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ketone bodies

explanation.summary: In prolonged fasting the brain shifts from glucose to ketone bodies for fuel.
explanation.whyCorrect: The organ fuel summary shows the brain uses glucose in the well-fed and fasting states but shifts to ketone bodies during prolonged fasting. This switch takes several days to develop and spares glucose for tissues that remain glucose-dependent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amino acids are mobilized for gluconeogenesis in the liver, not oxidized directly by the brain as its main fuel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Free fatty acids do not readily cross the blood-brain barrier and are not the brain's fuel in starvation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose fuels the brain in the well-fed and short-term fasting states, but is largely replaced by ketones in prolonged fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycerol serves as a hepatic gluconeogenic substrate, not a direct brain fuel.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: In the liver during a fast, glucagon activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates glycogen synthase. What is the effect of this phosphorylation on glycogen synthase activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates glycogen synthase only in skeletal muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It activates glycogen synthase, increasing glycogen synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts glycogen synthase into phosphorylase kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has no effect because glycogen synthase is not a PKA target

choices.label: E
choices.text: It inactivates glycogen synthase, inhibiting glycogen synthesis

explanation.summary: Glucagon-driven PKA phosphorylation inactivates glycogen synthase, halting glycogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucagon works through cAMP and PKA to phosphorylate glycogen synthase, which inactivates it and inhibits glycogen synthesis. This complements PKA phosphorylation of phosphorylase kinase and glycogen phosphorylase, which together promote glycogen degradation during fasting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The inactivating effect is not restricted to skeletal muscle, and the liver is the site described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phosphorylation of glycogen synthase inactivates the anabolic enzyme; insulin (via dephosphorylation) is what activates it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphorylation modifies glycogen synthase's activity; it does not transform it into a different enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycogen synthase is a genuine PKA target, and its phosphorylation is a key step in switching off glycogenesis.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A researcher compares fuel use across metabolic states. Which of the following cell types relies on glucose across the well-fed, fasting, AND prolonged fasting states without ever switching to an alternative fuel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adipocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cardiac muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells

explanation.summary: Red blood cells use glucose in every metabolic state, including prolonged fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: The organ fuel table lists red blood cells as using glucose in the well-fed, fasting, and prolonged fasting states. Lacking mitochondria, RBCs cannot oxidize fatty acids or ketone bodies and remain obligately glucose-dependent throughout.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipocytes use glucose when well-fed but rely on fatty acids during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brain uses glucose when well-fed and fasting but shifts to ketone bodies in prolonged fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cardiac muscle uses fatty acids when well-fed and shifts to fatty acids plus ketone bodies during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver uses predominately glucose when well-fed but switches to fatty acids during fasting.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman finishes lunch at 12:30 PM. Which of the following time periods best corresponds to the fed (absorptive) state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any period after food intake has ceased for 2-4 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: From approximately 4 hours after the meal until the next meal

choices.label: C
choices.text: From the end of the meal until approximately 3-4 hours later

choices.label: D
choices.text: The interval during which the meal itself is being consumed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The overnight period of sleep before the next morning's meal

explanation.summary: The fed (absorptive, post-prandial) state spans the window from the end of a meal until roughly 3-4 hours afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: The absorptive or post-prandial state encompasses the window from when a meal is finished for about 3-4 hours after. During this time insulin signaling predominates and nutrients are moved into storage depots.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cessation of intake for about 2-4 days defines the prolonged fasting (starvation) state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No meal for about 4 hours defines the fasting (post-absorptive) state, not the fed state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prandial refers to the actual consumption of the meal itself, not the absorptive window that follows.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An overnight fast during sleep places the body in the basal metabolic state, a post-absorptive state.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes routine screening. After an overnight fast, her plasma glucose is 118 mg/dL, and the value is confirmed on repeat testing. Based on standard fasting plasma glucose ranges, which of the following best classifies this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diabetic fasting value (overt disease)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypoglycemic fasting value (below range)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal fasting value (no impairment)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal post-prandial value (after eating)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pre-diabetic (initial impairment)

explanation.summary: A fasting plasma glucose of 101-125 mg/dL falls in the pre-diabetic (initial impairment) range.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal fasting glucose is 70-100 mg/dL, pre-diabetic (initial impairment) is 101-125 mg/dL, and diabetic is greater than 126 mg/dL. A confirmed fasting value of 118 mg/dL lies within the pre-diabetic range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The diabetic fasting threshold is greater than 126 mg/dL, which 118 mg/dL does not reach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypoglycemia is a fasting value below the 70-100 mg/dL normal range; 118 mg/dL is elevated, not low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal fasting glucose is 70-100 mg/dL; 118 mg/dL exceeds this range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The value was obtained after an overnight fast, so post-prandial ranges (170-200 mg/dL normal) do not apply.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A healthy 28-year-old man eats dinner at 7 PM, sleeps through the night, and wakes at 6 AM before eating anything. Which of the following terms best describes his metabolic state upon waking?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorptive state

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basal metabolic state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-prandial state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prandial state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged fasting state

explanation.summary: An overnight fast during sleep places the body in the basal metabolic state, one of the post-absorptive states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fasting begins when no meal has been consumed for about 4 hours. An overnight fast while one sleeps puts the body into what is referred to as the basal metabolic state, and these fasting periods are collectively known as the post-absorptive states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The absorptive state lasts only about 3-4 hours after a meal ends and has long since passed by 6 AM.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Post-prandial is synonymous with the absorptive window of about 3-4 hours after eating, which ended before midnight.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prandial refers to the actual consumption of a meal, which is not occurring on waking.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonged fasting (starvation) requires cessation of food intake for about 2-4 days, not a single night.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with an insulin-secreting tumor develops confusion, slurred speech, and dizziness whenever his plasma glucose falls. Which of the following best explains why the central nervous system is the first system to manifest symptoms when blood glucose cannot be maintained?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neurons lack glucose transporters and rely on passive diffusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: The brain cannot perform glycolysis and depends on the TCA cycle alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: The brain depends exclusively on fatty acid oxidation for ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: The brain lacks mitochondria and cannot oxidize acetyl-CoA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The brain neither stores glycogen nor synthesizes its own glucose

explanation.summary: The brain does not store glycogen or make glucose, so it depends on circulating glucose and is vulnerable to hypoglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The metabolically active CNS relies heavily on glycolysis and the TCA cycle for ATP. Because the brain itself does not store glycogen or make glucose, it is reliant on circulating glucose, and any disruption in glucose maintenance first manifests with CNS symptoms such as confusion, slurred speech, and dizziness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain takes up circulating glucose readily; its vulnerability stems from lacking its own reserves, not from lacking transport.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The CNS relies heavily on glycolysis together with the TCA cycle for ATP production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brain uses glucose in the fed and fasting states and can switch to ketone bodies in prolonged fasting, not fatty acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brain has mitochondria and uses the TCA cycle; it is the absence of glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis that creates dependence on blood glucose.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes injects her usual insulin dose but skips breakfast. Two hours later she is shaky, anxious, and sweating profusely. The diaphoresis is most directly attributable to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of circulating ketone bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol-induced gene expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct action of insulin on sweat glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucagon release from pancreatic α-cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of adrenaline (epinephrine)

explanation.summary: Diaphoresis during hypoglycemia is sweating driven by adrenaline.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low blood glucose is associated with confusion, irritability or anxiety, headache, dizziness/shakiness, slurred speech, diaphoresis, seizures, and coma. The diaphoresis is specifically described as sweating from adrenaline, which is released as part of the response to hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ketone bodies become a brain fuel only after several days of fasting and do not cause sweating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol acts through intracellular receptors to alter gene expression over time and is not the source of acute sweating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin caused the hypoglycemia, but the sweating is attributed to adrenaline, not to insulin acting on sweat glands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucagon mobilizes hepatic glucose during hypoglycemia but is not the mediator of diaphoresis.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: Two patients present to a clinic on the same afternoon. One has a plasma glucose of 45 mg/dL and is nearly comatose; the other has a fasting plasma glucose of 165 mg/dL and reports feeling entirely well. Which of the following best explains this contrast?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hyperglycemic damage accrues unfelt over time, whereas modest hypoglycemia acutely impairs the brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin secretion ceases at high glucose, sparing the brain from the effects of glucose excess

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ketone bodies immediately replace glucose as brain fuel whenever glucose rises above normal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal excretion of glucose neutralizes hyperglycemia before it can cause any harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skeletal muscle glycogen buffers high glucose but cannot be released to correct low glucose

explanation.summary: The low glucose range is narrow and acutely symptomatic, whereas hyperglycemia damages tissues over time without being felt.
explanation.whyCorrect: The low range of blood glucose is far more confined and less varied than the high range. A drop of only a few increments of 10 mg/dL below normal can render a person comatose, whereas the same degree of elevation is fairly inconsequential in the moment. Hyperglycemic states manifest damage (for example vascular) over time, and the person is usually unaware and does not feel the elevation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin is secreted in response to high glucose, not stopped by it, and the asymptomatic nature of hyperglycemia reflects slow, unperceived damage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brain's switch to ketone bodies takes several days of prolonged fasting and is unrelated to elevated glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperglycemia is not harmless; it causes damage such as vascular injury over time, it is simply not felt acutely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle glycogen never contributes to circulating glucose and is not the reason hyperglycemia is asymptomatic.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: A physiologist compares glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscle of a healthy adult. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Total glycogen mass and glycogen concentration per tissue mass are both greatest in skeletal muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Total glycogen mass and glycogen concentration per tissue mass are both greatest in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Total glycogen mass is greatest in adipose tissue, but concentration per tissue mass is greatest in the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total glycogen mass is greatest in skeletal muscle, but concentration per tissue mass is greatest in the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total glycogen mass is greatest in the liver, but concentration per tissue mass is greatest in skeletal muscle

explanation.summary: Skeletal muscle holds the bulk of body glycogen because of its mass, but the liver has the highest glycogen concentration per tissue mass.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two predominant sites where glycogen is synthesized, stored, and degraded are the liver and skeletal muscle. The bulk of glycogen is within skeletal muscle due to its extensive bodily mass; however, the highest concentration of glycogen per tissue mass is found in the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Skeletal muscle holds the most total glycogen, but its concentration per tissue mass is lower than the liver's.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The liver wins on concentration, but skeletal muscle contains the greater total mass of glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adipose tissue stores triglycerides, not glycogen; glycogen depots are the liver and skeletal muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the relationship: muscle has the greater total mass and liver the greater concentration.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State

questions.stem: In an isolated skeletal muscle preparation with no hormonal input and with Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum pharmacologically blocked, repeated contraction still activates glycogen phosphorylase. Which of the following best explains this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AMP produced by adenylate kinase allosterically activates the enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calmodulin binds and activates phosphorylase kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: cAMP generated by adenylate cyclase activates protein kinase A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate accumulates and allosterically activates the enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin-dependent phosphatases dephosphorylate the enzyme

explanation.summary: Contraction generates AMP via adenylate kinase, and AMP allosterically activates muscle glycogen phosphorylase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscle glycogen reserves are degraded upon activity/contraction via the production of AMP, which allosterically activates glycogen phosphorylase.
